paragraphs: The man on the other side of the table was holding his departure permit in both hands, the way you hold a plate that is too full.
"Keep it on you until you reach the station," said Kask.
"They'll ask for it at every checkpoint.
The convoy leaves the day after tomorrow at six.
Be there an hour early."
The man nodded.
He was fifty-two, with a housing debt taken on eleven years ago and never repaid, a wife who had left, no children.
Kask knew all this because it was written in file R-87990, and because he had spent three days verifying it.
The interview room was white and windowless.
A table, two chairs, a ceiling light that hummed on a very low note.
"And afterwards?" the man asked.
"After the Gate."
"After the Gate, you're no longer under the City's jurisdiction."
"But what's there?"
Kask had heard the question four hundred times, give or take.
He always gave the same answer, because it was the only one he knew.
"Something else," he said.
"Another life."
He stood up, which meant the interview was over.
The man stood too, a little too quickly, and tucked the permit into the inside pocket of his jacket.
At the door, Kask held out his hand.
It was the only part of the interview that wasn't in the procedure, and he did it anyway.
"Bon voyage," he said.
The man shook his hand and left.
Kask stayed standing in the white room for a moment, then opened the file on his terminal and entered the time of issue: 10:14.
He filed it.
In two days, at 10:14, the Registry would stop recognizing R-87990.
His doors would no longer open, his money would cease to exist, his name would be removed from the lists.
Nobody said he was being erased.
They said his file was being rectified.
It was more accurate, and Kask liked words to be accurate.
The Rectification Bureau occupied floors fourteen to twenty-one of a tower in Sector 2.
Kask had worked on the sixteenth for eleven years.
He had never been above the nineteenth, or below the fourteenth.
The other floors belonged to other departments: Transport, which ran the convoys; Sanitation, which maintained the abandoned levels; others whose names he knew without knowing what they did.
The departments didn't talk to each other.
Each received what it had to process and passed on what it had processed.
Kask found that healthy.
A man who sees everything does nothing properly.
That day there was a send-off on the sixteenth.
Halm was retiring after thirty-one years of service.
Two desks had been pushed against the wall, with paper cups on them and a bottle of pale wine.
Dross came down from her floor for the occasion.
She gave a short speech, in a calm voice, about rigor and loyalty, and about a city that stood upright thanks to men like Halm.
Then she handed him an envelope.
Halm took it with an emotion he made no effort to hide.
His eyes were wet.
Everyone applauded.
Kask applauded too.
He watched Halm and felt something like envy, without it being quite that.
Thirty-one years, then an envelope, then nothing.
No more files.
No more white room.
He tried to picture what Halm would do the next morning, at the hour he would have taken the metro, and couldn't.
"Thinking about it already?" said a voice beside him.
It was Teodor, a cup in his hand.
Kask had trained him three years ago.
Teodor was good: methodical, discreet, he didn't ask pointless questions.
Kask had taught him that first.
"I've got twenty years left," said Kask.
"You'll hold out."
"Yes," said Kask.
"I'll hold out."
He walked home, as he did every evening.
The shortest route to his lodgings in Sector 9 took twenty-five minutes.
He took forty, because he went by Alley 11-C.
Alley 11-C had nothing to recommend it.
It ran along the edge of Sector 14, between blackened concrete facades, and led nowhere you couldn't reach some other way.
Halfway along there was a closed café whose sign only half lit up anymore.
Kask didn't know why he went that way.
He had noticed it one day in the spring and promised himself he would take the direct route the next day.
The next day, he took Alley 11-C.
He had given up trying to understand.
On evenings when he forced himself not to go that way, he came home with a kind of tightness in his chest, as if he had left a door open behind him.
In the street, people stepped aside.
It was nothing dramatic.
A woman crossing to the other pavement, a man lowering his eyes, a conversation breaking off as he passed.
The long dark coat, the administrative cut, the small grey badge on the lapel: everyone knew what they meant.
Kask no longer noticed.
He walked with his hands in his pockets, and he hummed.
He always hummed the same tune.
A few notes that rose and then came down again, and that stopped at roughly the same place, as if he didn't know how it ended.
He had no idea where it came from.
He had never heard it on the radio, or anywhere public.
He only realized he was doing it when he stopped, and each time he was a little surprised to have been humming.
His lodgings were Bureau housing, assigned to him, on the ninth floor of a building where only agents lived.
Two rooms.
A bed, a table, two chairs, a wardrobe, a terminal.
The walls were pale grey and he had never repainted them.
There were no photographs, no ornaments, no plants.
Anyone who walked in would have learned nothing about him, except that he was tidy.
Kask knew this and it didn't bother him.
He owned only one book.
An Atlas of Lighthouses, old, its binding worn, which described one by one the lighthouses of a coast he had never seen and never would.
He no longer remembered when he had bought it.
Some evenings he read it at random, a page or two.
The height of the tower, the range of the light, the rhythm of the flashes.
He found it soothing.
In the table drawer there was also a key.
A flat, old-fashioned metal key, the kind people used before the Registry.
He had found it in the spring, slipped into the binding of the Atlas, the evening the spine had finally come unstuck.
It opened nothing in his home.
In the upper City, no door opened with a key anymore.
He should have thrown it away.
He had put it in the drawer, and there it had stayed.
That evening he didn't read.
He sat at the table, in front of the dark terminal, and stayed motionless for a long time.
It happened to him more and more often.
He wasn't tired.
He wasn't sad, or if he was, it was a sadness without an object, unlike any he knew.
It was more like an absence.
A place inside him where something should have been.
The Bureau doctor had called it service fatigue and prescribed regulators.
He took them.
They changed nothing, but he took them.
The next day he had an existence check in Sector 9.
The procedure was old and Kask respected it.

Before any rectification, the agent had to verify with his own eyes that the subject existed exactly as the Registry described: that they lived at the stated address, that they matched their photograph, that there had been no mistake about the person.
It usually took an hour or two.
All you had to do was watch.
The subject was Ivane Morr.
Thirty-eight, warehouse worker, consumer debt.
Kask waited for her on a bench facing the entrance to her building, his terminal on his knees.
She came out at 8:02.
He recognized her immediately: the same woman as in the photograph, paler, a bag on her shoulder.
She stopped at the edge of the pavement to let a delivery rider pass.
The wind blew a strand of hair across her face.
She tucked it back behind her ear with two fingers.
Kask stopped breathing.
There was nothing about her that could explain it.
She wasn't beautiful, he wasn't attracted to her, she didn't remind him of anyone.
He could have passed her a thousand times without seeing her.
It wasn't her.
It was the gesture, or not even the gesture: something inside him that had given way at the moment of the gesture, like a missing step underfoot in the dark.
He felt his heart beating in his throat.
His hands were cold on the terminal.
The woman crossed and disappeared around the corner.
Kask stayed where he was.
He didn't know for how long.
When he looked up, the bench opposite was in the sun, and it hadn't been when he sat down.
He wrote his report.
Subject consistent with Registry.
Address verified.
No anomalies.
He sent it at 9:47, when he should have left at 9:07.
Forty minutes late.
It had never happened to him in eleven years.
He didn't think about it again.
The next ten days were ordinary.
He issued Ivane Morr her departure permit, in the white room, and wished her bon voyage; she had no effect on him at all.
He processed two other files.
He took his regulators.
He went home every evening by Alley 11-C.
Halm didn't come back to the sixteenth, and his desk was given to someone else.
On the evening of November 12th, at 23:40, his terminal gave the short tone that announced a service notification.
Kask was already in bed.
He got up, because he always got up, and switched on the screen.
It was an assignment notice, like the ones he received every week.
The usual format.
The file number, the name of the assigned agent, the grounds, the filing date, the deadline.
The subject's name was his own.
File R-88412.
Subject: KASK.
Assigned agent: TEODOR.
Grounds: voluntary request (form 7-B).
Filing date: June 14.
Statutory deadline: 48 hours.
Kask read the notice once, slowly, the way he read every notice.
Then he did what he would have done for any file: he checked the fields, one by one.
The registration number was his.
So was the date of birth, and the address of his Bureau lodgings, and the number of his badge.
There was no namesake.
There was no data-entry error.
The June 14th the notice referred to was the previous year's, seventeen months ago.
He opened the attachment.
Form 7-B was a one-page document he knew by heart without ever having processed more than a handful: nobody asked for their own rectification, or almost nobody.
At the top, the applicant's identity.
In the middle, a line for the reason, left blank, which was permitted.
At the bottom, a statement that the request was irrevocable, then the signature.
It was his.
There was no doubt about it.
He recognized the slant of the letters, the too-tight loop of the K, and above all the 7 in the date, crossed through the middle with a small horizontal stroke.
He had crossed his sevens since childhood.
He didn't know anyone else who did.
He switched off the screen and sat in the dark.
He had never filled in a 7-B.
He was as certain of it as one is of one's own name.
He searched his memory for June 14th of the previous year and found nothing, which proved nothing: who remembers a particular day, seventeen months later?
He went back to bed.
He didn't sleep.
Around three, he caught himself humming, stopped, and listened to the silence of the building.
At the kiosk on the ground floor, where he bought a coffee every morning, the payment terminal showed a red rectangle.
"Declined," said the vendor, without looking at him.
Kask knew the procedure.
During the statutory deadline, which the regulations called the settling period, the subject's access fell away in stages.
First, convenience access: kiosks, vending machines, leisure venues.
Then transport.
Then money.
Then housing.
An agent's badge, when there was one, went last.
The staging was supposed to give the subject time to settle their affairs.
Kask had explained it to hundreds of people, in the white room, in a measured voice.
He thanked the vendor and left without coffee.
The metro, at least, let him through.
In the carriage, a woman got up to change seats.
He didn't look at her.
On the sixteenth, his badge opened the door as usual.
Nobody looked up when he came in.
Nobody looked up when he crossed the open-plan floor either, and it was that, more than anything, that made him understand that everyone knew.
Assignment notices weren't public.
But at the Bureau, you quickly learned to read what wasn't written.
Teodor was waiting at his desk.
File R-88412 was open on his screen.
He had the drawn look of a man who hadn't slept well either.
"I got it last night," he said quietly.
"I don't understand."
"Neither do I."
Teodor glanced around them, then scrolled down to the processing history.
He put his finger on a line.
"Look."
Below the filing date there was a stamp: SUSPENDED.
A date, one month after filing.
And next to it, the signatory's code, replaced by a row of grey squares.
Masked at Teodor's clearance level.
At Kask's too, no doubt.
"It stayed suspended for sixteen months," said Teodor.
"And it was reactivated two days ago.
I've never seen that."
Nor had Kask.
He looked at the grey squares for a long time.
"I'm not going to take it on," said Teodor.
"I'll send it back.
I'll say there's a conflict of interest."
"No."
"Kask…"
"You don't argue with a 7-B," said Kask.
"I taught you that.
If you send it back, they'll ask you why, and you won't have an answer.
If you refuse a 7-B, you're the one who gets rectified.
Sign the acceptance."
Teodor didn't move.
"Sign it,"
Kask repeated.
"I'll deal with it."
He would deal with it.
During the night he had had time to think, and thinking had calmed him.
A 7-B was irrevocable.
But a forged 7-B wasn't a 7-B: it was a forgery, and a forgery was void.
The Bureau couldn't execute a procedural defect.
If he could prove the signature wasn't his, the file would collapse on its own.
He had forty-seven hours left.
"I need the filing receipt," he said.
"I don't have access to it.
You do."
Teodor hesitated, then nodded.
He signed the acceptance.
Dross's office was on the twenty-first floor, the top of the Bureau.
Kask had been up there only three times in eleven years.
You reached it by a separate lift, which opened onto a carpeted corridor where you could hear nothing.
The room was large and quiet.
Green plants along the picture window, the City below, grey all the way to the horizon.
Dross poured him tea without asking whether he wanted any.
She was about sixty, with short white hair and economical gestures.
"I know why you're here," she said.
"Sit down."
He sat.
"I never signed that form."
"The signature is yours.
I checked."
"It looks like mine."
Dross took a sip of tea.
"You asked for it, Kask.
Seventeen months ago.
I understand that you don't remember.
People do things, at certain moments, and they forget them.
It's not a reproach."
"Why was it suspended?"
"I don't know," she said.
"I only see what the Registry shows me.
An administrative delay, probably.
It happens."
"Sixteen months."
"It happens."
There was a silence.
Through the picture window, a Transport convoy could be seen gliding slowly along an elevated track, westward, toward the Gate.
"A 7-B can't be withdrawn,"
Dross said gently.
"You know that better than anyone.
It's even what gives it its dignity: it's the one decision you make once and for all.
I find that beautiful, in a way."
She set down her cup.
"Are you sleeping well, these days?"
The question was harmless.
He said yes.
She smiled, the way you smile at someone telling a polite lie, and walked him back to the lift.
That evening, the metro gate refused his badge.
He walked home.
He went by Alley 11-C, past the closed café with its sputtering sign, and didn't even wonder why.
The door of his lodgings opened.
He switched on the terminal and looked up his service calendar for June 14th of the previous year.
He expected to find a file, an appointment, some sign of what he had done that day.
The day was empty.
Not a file, not a meeting, not a line.
The 13th was full, and so was the 15th.
June 14th was blank.
He tried to open his own personnel file with his agent access, which still worked.
The terminal displayed a message he himself had read out to others, long ago, when they tried:
Agents may not consult their own file.
He switched off the screen.
In the drawer, the key hadn't moved.
For the first time in eleven years, Kask wondered what a man could want to escape so badly that he would sign his own disappearance.
The money went during the night.
In the morning, in place of his balance, the terminal showed a line he had never seen from this side of the screen: Account being closed.
He washed, shaved, dressed.
The coat, the badge.
Before going out, he opened the table drawer and took the key.
He didn't ask himself why.
He slipped it into his pocket and shut the door behind him.
Teodor was waiting at the foot of the building, in the cold, hands deep in his pockets.
He didn't say good morning.
He held out a sheet of paper folded in four.
Paper: nobody at the Bureau printed anything anymore, and Kask understood that Teodor had chosen to let nothing go through the network.
It was the filing receipt.
A few lines, in administrative format.
Form 7-B.
Filed at: public terminal PB-14/3-07.
Sector 14, Level −3.
Validation: handwritten signature.
"Level −3 of Sector 14," said Teodor.
"There's nothing down there.
They're decommissioned levels, under Sanitation.
Why would there be a working terminal?"
"There are terminals everywhere.
Nobody takes them out."
"Have you ever been there?"
"Never."
He said it without hesitation, and he believed it.
Teodor looked at him for a moment, then turned his eyes to the street.
"What are you going to do?"
"Check."
It was what he had been doing for eleven years.
He folded the sheet and put it in his coat pocket, with the key.
He walked.
Without transport, it took more than an hour to reach Sector 14, and he took the route he knew best, the one from his evenings: Sector 11, then Alley 11-C.
He passed the closed café.
The sign was dark at this hour.
He kept going to the end of the alley, where he usually turned back, where it lost itself against a concrete wall.
He had never looked at that wall.
He looked at it now.
On the left, in a recess, there was a wire-mesh door, half open, and behind it a service stairway going down.
A faded Sanitation sign read: Sector 14.
Lower levels.
No entry.
Kask stood still in front of the door.
Every evening since the spring, perhaps longer, he had made this detour without knowing why.
He had walked fifteen minutes too far to arrive in front of this wall, and he had turned back.
He understood, with a slowness that frightened him, that Alley 11-C didn't lead nowhere.
It led here.
He hadn't been strolling.
He had been following a path, and every evening he had stopped one step short of the end.
He pushed the door and went down.
The stairs turned on themselves, level after level.
At Level −1, the light from the tubes went yellowish.
At Level −2, half of them were dead.
The air smelled of wet metal and dust.
At Level −3, the stairs opened onto a low gallery, wider than he would have thought, with cables running along the ceiling.
It wasn't abandoned.
There were footprints in the dust, recent rubbish, and somewhere far off, the sound of a machine.
Terminal PB-14/3-07 stood about thirty metres from the foot of the stairs.
An old model, pale green, its screen scratched.
It was still powered.
Kask laid his hand on it.
It was warm.
He felt nothing in particular.
No memory surfaced.
There was only, once again, that dull tightness in his chest, the same as on evenings when he didn't go by the alley.
He knew Vay's name the way he knew many names: from files.
It turned up in a dozen of them, always in the margins, always in the same place.
An identity broker, who sold fragments of dead files to the living.
The Bureau knew about him and let him be, because he operated where the Registry didn't look, and what isn't looked at doesn't exist.
According to the files, he ran a repair shop on Level −3 of Sector 14.
Kask found it at the end of the gallery, behind a curtain of plastic strips.
A workshop cluttered with gutted terminals, screens, boxes of components.
A thin man was bent over a workbench, a loupe screwed into one eye.
He looked up when Kask came in, took out the loupe, and looked at him without surprise.
"Kask," he said.
Kask hadn't given him his name.
"You know me."
"Everyone knows the coats," said Vay.
"You, I know a little better.
What do you want?"
"My personnel file.
All of it.
I'm not allowed to consult it with my access."
"No.
But with your access, I can."
Vay held out his hand, palm open.
"Your badge.
One hour.
I do what I need to do, and then I pull your file for you."
"What you need to do?"
"That's none of your business.
That's the price.
You don't have any money anymore, anyway."
Kask looked at the outstretched hand.
His agent's badge was the last access he had left, and one of the most closely watched in the City.
What a man like Vay could do with it in an hour, he preferred not to imagine.
He thought of the crossed 7 at the bottom of the form.
He unpinned the badge from his lapel and put it in Vay's hand.
Vay disappeared into the back room.
Kask waited on a stool, among the dead screens, listening to the distant sound of the machine.
He never found out what Vay had looked for.
When he came back, Vay turned a screen toward him.
"There's your file.
Look at last year, mostly."
It was an agent's file like any other.
The evaluations, all excellent.
The files processed, year by year.
The medical checks.
And, the previous year, between mid-March and mid-July, a greyed-out stretch of four months, with a single entry:
Period rectified.
Protocol D.
Agent fit to resume duty.
Kask knew Protocol D the way you know a rumour.
People spoke of it in low voices on the sixteenth, about agents who had "aged badly" or who had processed one file too many.
They called it decompression.
They said it brought relief.
They never said exactly what it took away.
"Four months," said Vay.
"You don't remember any of it, do you?"
Kask didn't answer.
"Something else," said Vay, taking the screen back.
"Someone paid me, for a year, to find out what had become of you.
Whether you were alive.
Whether you were still working.
How you were.
I gave them news once a month."
"Who?"
"That's not mine to say.
They stopped paying four months ago."
He handed back the badge.
The little grey light on the side was still on.
Then he took a scrap of cardboard from the bench, scribbled something, and held it out.
"Go to this address.
Tonight."
Level −4.
Founders' Passage.
Building 6.
Third floor.
"How do I get in?"
"Down there, the buildings are older than the Registry," said Vay.
"The doors still have locks."
In his pocket, Kask's hand closed around the key.
"Tonight,"
Vay repeated.
"Not tomorrow."
He went back out into the gallery.
He stood for a long time near the terminal, without touching it.
His plan fit in one sentence: prove the signature was forged.
He had believed in it all night, all morning.
He was still clinging to it on the way down the stairs.
But four months of his life had been taken from him, and the signature fell right in the middle of those four months.
A man who doesn't remember signing hasn't necessarily signed nothing.
He knew that.
He had explained it to others.
Further along the gallery, a narrower stairway went down again.
Kask turned up the collar of his coat and started down it.
He had expected ruins.
The stairs came out onto a street.
A real street, narrow, under a concrete ceiling so high you could barely make it out, between two rows of old buildings with lit windows.
Cables strung from one facade to the other carried bare bulbs.
There were stalls at street level, workshops open to the pavement, a smell of hot oil and solder.
Someone was hammering metal.
Further on, behind a fogged window, rows of plants were growing under violet lamps.
People lived here.
They came and went, carried bags, talked on doorsteps.
A man was pushing a cart of spare parts.
Two children ran past.
Nobody paid with a terminal: Kask saw paper notes passing from hand to hand, objects traded for other objects.
Nobody wore a badge, and no door opened by itself.
He knew, like everyone up above, that the lower levels were empty.
It was written in the Sanitation reports.
He had read those reports without thinking about them, the way you read the weather.
They noticed him at once.
The coat, the cut, the badge: he was as visible here as a siren.
Conversations stopped as he passed, and didn't start again.
A woman grabbed one of the children by the arm and pulled him inside.
A man sitting in front of a workshop got up without a word and shut his door.
Another spat on the ground, right in front of his feet, without taking his eyes off him.
Up above, people avoided him.
Down here, they hated him, and nobody bothered to hide it.
Kask kept walking, Vay's scrap of cardboard in one hand.
In an open workshop, a man of about fifty was repairing a stove.
He had a hollow face and glasses mended with thread.
Kask slowed down without knowing why.
He felt he had seen him before.
Not in the street, not by chance.
There was something specific in that face, like a word on the tip of the tongue.
A photograph, perhaps.
A corridor.
The man looked up.
He looked at Kask for a long time, and Kask saw that he recognized him.
Him.
Without hesitation.
The man said nothing.
He put down his tools, very slowly, and waited for Kask to pass.
A little further on, it was a woman at a first-floor window who drew the curtain when she saw him.
Then an old man sitting on a step, who gave him a small nod, ironic, almost polite.
Each time, the same impression: he had seen these people somewhere.
Each time, he couldn't put a name to them.
And each time, they knew who he was.
An idea began to take shape in his mind.
He pushed it away.
It came back.
He pushed it away again, because it was absurd, because the rectified left, because he had watched the convoys pulling away toward the Gate from the picture window on the twenty-first floor.
He walked faster.
Founders' Passage was a curving lane that smelled of coal.
Building 6 was the last one, a dark brick structure with a heavy wooden door.
There was no reader, no camera.
Only a brass lock, worn in the middle.
Kask took the key out of his pocket.
It went in first time.
It turned without forcing, with a clean dry click, and the door opened.
He stayed on the threshold.
His hands were damp.
He thought of the binding of the Atlas, of the drawer, of the months this key had waited beside him without his knowing what it was for.
Then he climbed the stairs.
On the third floor, the same key opened the only door on the landing.
The flat was empty.
Nobody there.
It was empty, but it was lived in, and Kask knew it as soon as he switched on the lamp.
A warm, orange light that existed nowhere up above.
A single large room, cluttered: rugs laid one over another, a sofa covered with a woven blanket, shelves made of planks and bricks, jars, dried herbs hanging by a small stove.
An old radio.
Objects mended, glued back together, repainted.
A cup left on the table, half full.
It smelled of spices and wood.
It was everything his own lodgings were not.
He touched nothing.
It was a professional reflex: you don't disturb the scene of a check.
He took a chair, set it facing the door, and sat down, his coat still on.
He waited.
Time passed.
The pipes of the old building knocked now and then.
In the lane, someone called a name he didn't catch.
The stove crackled faintly.
Kask looked at the room the way he would have looked at any room, noting what he saw.
That was how he saw the book.
It was on the nearest shelf, lying on its side.
An Atlas of Lighthouses, the same edition as his, the same faded blue cover.
He got up, took it, opened it at random.
The margins were covered in pencil notes.
Remarks about the lighthouses, distances, questions.
Range: 17 miles.
Too far to see from here?
The 7 was crossed with a small horizontal stroke.
It was his handwriting.
He had no memory of writing it.
He put the book back exactly where it had been.
As he turned, he saw the wall above the table, which he hadn't looked at when he came in.
A large sheet was pinned to it.
A map drawn by hand, in felt pen, with care.
A tower marked with a cross: the Bureau, Sector 2.
A line that went down, crossed Sector 9, ran along Sector 11, entered Alley 11-C, passed a small square labelled café, and stopped at a stairway.
It was his detour.
The same one, to the metre.
Kask sat back down.
He laid his hands flat on his knees to stop them shaking.
He didn't understand.
There was nothing in his memory, nothing, and yet his whole body was as tense as it had been on the bench in Sector 9, the morning of the strand of hair.
He waited some more.
He heard footsteps on the stairs.
The door opened on a woman carrying a canvas bag.
She stopped dead on the threshold.
She was perhaps thirty-five.
Brown hair tied back in a hurry, a jacket too big for her, hands worn by work.
She looked at him, and Kask saw that she recognized him.
Not the way the man with the stove had.
Differently.
Her face came apart, for barely a second, then closed again.
He looked at her and felt nothing in particular.
A stranger.
Only that underlying unease, the same as always, a little stronger.
She saw it.
She saw that he didn't recognize her.
Kask understood, later, that this was what had hurt her most: not his being there, but his empty gaze.
She put the bag down.
She closed the door behind her, without hurrying.
"Sixteen months," she said.
Her voice was low, very calm.
"Who are you?"
Kask asked.
She didn't answer.
"How is it that I have the key to your place?
Why is that book…"
"Be quiet," she said.
"Please."
He was quiet.
She crossed the room, knelt in front of a low shelf and took out a tin box, the kind once used for biscuits.
She opened it.
Inside was a small recorder, an old grey model, barely bigger than a pack of cards.
She put it on the table in front of him.
"You told me to give you this," she said.
"If one day you came back without knowing who I was."
She looked at him a moment longer, the way you look at a place you once lived in that has been sold.
Then she picked up her jacket, opened the door, and went out.
He heard her going down the stairs.
Kask was left alone with the recorder.
There was a single button.
Kask pressed it.
A breath, first.
The sound of a room, perhaps this one.
Then a voice.
He didn't recognize it right away.
It was a tired voice, a little hoarse, speaking slowly, choosing its words.
It took him several seconds to understand that it was his own.
It sounded like the one he heard in his head, and at the same time it didn't: it was more alive.
"If you're listening to this, it means they've put you through Protocol D.
I don't know what you'll have left.
I'll do it like a report.
In order.
It's June 14th.
I'm at her place.
Her name is Nell.
Two years ago, I processed a debt file.
A man of twenty-six.
I issued him his departure permit, I wished him bon voyage, he boarded the convoy.
He had promised to write to his sister once he got there.
She waited.
She wrote to the Bureau, four times, asking for news of him.
The letters reached the sixteenth.
Nobody answered them.
I read them.
I filed them.
In March, a 7-B came in to the sixteenth.
I recognized the address.
It was hers.
She wanted to leave to find him.
I asked to handle the file.
I'm not quite sure why.
I think I already had doubts.
I think I'd had doubts since the letters.
I did the existence check.
I spoke to her.
I wasn't allowed to.
I saw her again.
I let the file drag.
(A silence.
The sound of breathing.)
We went down, she and I.
By the stairs at the end of the alley.
Down there I saw people I had rectified.
Dozens of them.
They didn't leave.
Nobody leaves.
The ones who board the convoy are never seen again.
Down here, everyone knows it.
Her brother boarded.
I went to see Brenn, too.
Retired three years ago, as they say.
He runs a counter in Sector 6.
He didn't recognize me.
He doesn't remember the Bureau.
Nobody retires.
They reassign us.
A rectifier doesn't resign.
They decompress him, and they put him somewhere else.
I'll do this job until I no longer know I've done it.
Nell's 7-B can't be withdrawn.
I can still hold it back a few weeks.
No more.
When it's executed, she won't board the convoy.
She'll stay here.
Tonight, I'm going to file mine.
At the terminal, at the foot of the stairs.
(Another silence, longer.)
I'm not leaving only for her.
I'm leaving because what I do is a horror, and they will never let me stop.
But I'm leaving for her too.
Above all for…
(The voice stops.
Resumes, drier.)
The key to her place is in the binding of the Atlas.
If they clean you out, they might not find it.
Never board the convoy.
You'll want to check all of this.
Check it.
And then, believe her."
A click.
Then nothing.
Kask stayed motionless on his chair.
He had just learned that he had loved someone.
He knew it now, the same way he knew things written in files: as information.
A date, a place, a reason.
There was nothing behind it.
Not a face, not a scene, not a gesture.
He had listened to a stranger with his voice saying things he couldn't bring himself to believe, and the stranger had been right about everything.
He played the recording again.
Then one passage, then another, going back, the way he would have reread a badly completed file looking for the error.
There was no error.
And yet something had changed.
It wasn't a memory.
It was the emptiness itself.
For sixteen months he had carried inside him a place without shape, an absence without a name.
Now the absence had an outline.
It was the size of a person.
And he understood that this was worse, and that it was better.
She came back an hour later.
He hadn't got up.
She sat down opposite him, on the other side of the table.
She looked at the recorder, then at his face, and she knew he had listened.
She knew too that it had brought nothing back.
She didn't cry.
She looked tired with a very old tiredness, one that had had time to settle in.
"Nell," he said.
The name meant nothing to him.
He said it anyway, to see.
"Don't do that," she said.
They sat for a while without speaking.
Then he asked what he hadn't dared ask himself in the street.
"The people down here.
The man with the stove.
The old man on the step."
"You know them," said Nell.
"You rectified them.
Not all of them you.
But you, or another coat.
They never left.
There is no elsewhere, Kask.
The ones who refuse to board the convoy come down here.
The ones who board are never seen again.
It's the one rule everyone knows, down here.
You never board the convoy."
He thought of the man in file R-87990, holding his permit in both hands.
He thought of Ivane Morr.
He thought of all the ones he had found reasonable, compliant, the ones who had asked for the exact time of the convoy and thanked him.
"The map, on the wall," he said.
"You drew it.
The first time you came.
You were afraid you wouldn't find your way back."
He looked at the felt-pen line, the little square marked café.
He didn't remember drawing it.
But his legs had remembered, every evening.
"Why didn't you come looking for me?"
She gave a short laugh, without joy.
"Come where?
Up there?
I don't have a name up there anymore.
No door opens for me.
An unattested woman in the upper City is an anomaly, and an anomaly gets reported.
Gets brought in.
You know very well where."
She folded her arms.
"I paid Vay.
For a year.
Once a month, he told me how you were.
You were fine.
You were working.
You were the best agent on the sixteenth.
You went home in the evenings."
"I didn't know."
"Neither did I.
I didn't know if you'd forgotten me or if you'd chosen to stay.
From a distance, they look the same."
She turned her eyes toward the stove.
"And if you had forgotten me, I was nothing to you anymore.
An unattested woman in front of a Bureau agent.
You'd have reported me.
It's your job."
He didn't answer, because she was right.
"Four months ago, I stopped paying," she said.
"I had to stop sometime."
Her voice cracked slightly on the last word, and she fell silent, and he saw that she was angry with herself for that small crack, as if he didn't deserve it.

She was still talking, later, about practical things: about Vay, about the water they diverted from a pipe on Level −3, about the work she did in a recycling workshop, when she broke off in the middle of a sentence.
She was looking at the lapel of his coat.
Kask looked down.
The little grey light on his badge had just gone out.
He looked at the time on the old radio. 23:40.
Forty-eight hours, to the minute, since the notification.
"There," said Nell.
He understood at once what it meant, because he had explained it four hundred times.
The Registry had just stopped recognizing him.
He could climb back up the stairs, the alley, the streets; nobody would stop him.
But up there, no door would open for him anymore.
Not his lodgings, not the Bureau, not the smallest gate.
He would be an anomaly.
Going back up no longer meant anything.
Kask looked at the small black rectangle on his lapel and thought, without knowing why, that he had just done, sixteen months late, exactly what he had planned.
She hadn't eaten.
Nor had he, since the day before.
She put water on the stove to heat, took vegetables from a basket, a piece of stale bread.
She didn't ask whether he was hungry.
She set out two plates.
He watched her from his chair.
It was the first time since the notification that he had seen someone go through ordinary motions without being afraid of him.
She chopped the vegetables quickly, on a battered board, her back to him.
And she was humming.
She probably didn't realize it.
A few notes that rose and then came down again.
Kask felt his heart tighten before he even understood.
It was his tune.
The one he had been humming for months in Alley 11-C, in the metro, in his lodgings, without knowing where it came from.
Without thinking, he began to hum it with her, very softly.
She stopped chopping.
Together they reached the place where Kask always stopped, where the tune seemed to lose itself.
He fell silent.
She didn't.
She went on, a few more notes, which came gently down and closed back on themselves.
The ending.
He had never known it.
She turned around.
"You never knew the end," she said.
"You always stopped there.
I was the one who sang it."
He found nothing to say.
He remembered nothing, not her, not this room, not the evenings they had sung this tune together.
But something in him remembered, something that wasn't his memory and that Protocol D hadn't known where to look for.
It was the only proof he ever had.
They ate without saying much.
He slept on the sofa.
She tossed him a blanket without a word and turned off the lamp.
He heard her lie down behind the curtain that divided the room in two, then nothing.
He woke in the middle of the night.
He didn't know what time it was.
The stove was still glowing.
On the other side of the curtain, Nell's breathing was slow and even.
He lay there listening to it, and he realized, with astonishment, that the empty place inside him was smaller.
It hadn't gone.
But for the first time in sixteen months, there was something beside it.
He fell asleep again.
It was the silence that woke him.
The background hum, the pipes and distant machines he had heard since he arrived without noticing anymore, had stopped.
The stove was out.
So was the stairwell bulb that showed under the door.
The whole sector had gone dark.
Nell was already up.
He sensed her more than saw her, by the window.
"Don't speak," she whispered.
He joined her.
At the end of the lane, where it met the main street, a white light had just come on.
Then another, further away.
Harsh beams sweeping the facades.
In their light moved figures in grey suits, helmeted, without any insignia.
Above them, at first-floor height, low drones glided, almost silent.
Nobody screamed.
That was the most terrible part.
Doors opened quietly, people came out running barefoot, without a word, and vanished into passages Kask couldn't see.
The Mutes knew this silence.
They knew what it meant.
"A collection," said Nell.
Kask was watching the lights.
He wasn't watching them the way Nell was.
He was watching them as an agent, and he understood before she did what they were doing.
He had read the Sanitation reports.
Dozens of them.
He had read them without thinking, the way you read the weather, because they were copied to the sixteenth.
They spoke of clean-up operations on decommissioned levels, carried out cell by cell, following the Registry grid.
Each cell was sealed from the outside, then processed, then the next, in numerical order.
North to south.
He looked at the lights, their positions, the order in which they had come on, and the grid drew itself in his head as clearly as on a screen.
"They're coming from the north," he said.
"They'll seal the main street first.
We need to go south.
Is there a way out that way?"
Nell looked at him in the dark.
"Through the cellars," she said.
For the first time in his life, what he knew about the system was helping him escape it.
They felt their way down the stairs.
Nell opened a low door on the ground floor, and they plunged into a maze of linked cellars that ran beneath the buildings of the lane.
Other shadows were already running through them.
They came up further on, in a courtyard, to the south.
From the courtyard, you could see the main street.
Kask stopped for a second, one second too long.
The vehicles were waiting in the middle of the street, headlights on.
Long pale-grey cars, windowless along the sides, with a small discreet emblem near the rear doors.
Kask knew them.
He had seen them hundreds of times from the picture window on the twenty-first floor, gliding along the elevated tracks toward the Gate.
They were the same.
The same cars as the Transport convoys.
Not similar cars: the same ones.
There weren't two systems.
There was only one.
People were being loaded into the back.
They hardly struggled.
Among them, Kask recognized the man with the stove, with his glasses mended with thread.
One of the men in grey pushed him in the back.
The glasses fell to the ground.
Nobody picked them up.
Nell pulled him by the sleeve.
They hid in a utility room at the end of a passage, between two dead electrical cabinets.
It was dark.
In the distance they could hear engines, footsteps, now and then a door being broken in.
Nell was breathing fast.
"You arrived yesterday," she said, very low.
"They arrive tonight."
He understood what she meant.
"It wasn't me."
"Are you sure?"
He wanted to say yes and couldn't.
He thought of his badge, left for an hour in Vay's hands.
Of what Vay had looked for in the back room.
Of the way he had repeated: Tonight.
Not tomorrow.
He didn't know.
He no longer knew anything about what he had done, or what had been done through him.
"I don't know," he said.
She didn't answer.
In the dark, he couldn't see her face.
They found them a little before dawn.
A team of three, in the passage.
A white light in their eyes, a calm voice, without anger, asking them to come out with their hands visible.
They came out.
One of the men in grey raised a small device to Nell's face.
The screen lit up green.
Unattested.
One more.
The man gestured toward the main street.
Then he raised the device to Kask's face.
The screen lit up orange.
The man frowned and read aloud, as if to make sure he had read it right:
"Subject reserved.
Directorate."
The Registry no longer recognized Kask.
Someone else did.
The three men looked at each other.
There was a second of hesitation, the kind Kask had learned to spot in people, on the sixteenth: the second when the procedure no longer says what to do.
He took a step sideways and placed himself between them and Nell.
"I'm the one you're looking for," he said.
"Not her."
Behind him, he felt Nell step back.
Then all he could hear were her footsteps, very fast, down the side passage.
One of the men moved as if to follow her.
The team leader stopped him with a gesture, his eyes on his orange screen.
The instruction was clear, and it spoke only of Kask.
They didn't put him in the grey cars.
They walked him to a small black vehicle parked apart, which looked like nothing he had seen that night.
They sat him in the back and closed the door.
The vehicle didn't move.
After a few minutes, the opposite door opened.
Someone got in and sat on the bench facing him.
A long dark coat, a grey badge on the lapel, its light glowing.
It was Teodor.
He said nothing.
Teodor said nothing for the whole journey.
The vehicle climbed by a service ramp Kask didn't know, crossed empty levels, then the upper City, still grey in the early morning.
Teodor looked out of the window.
Only once did he turn his eyes toward Kask's lapel, toward the small black rectangle of his badge, and he looked away at once.
At the foot of the Sector 2 tower, the doors didn't open for Kask.
They opened for Teodor, and Kask passed behind him, like an object being carried.
In the separate lift that went up to the twenty-first, he saw their reflection in the metal wall: two identical coats, two men, only one of whom existed.
Dross was waiting for him.
The sun was rising behind the picture window and laid a pink light over the plants.
She had made tea.
She signalled to Teodor to leave, and Teodor left.
"Sit down, Kask."
He sat.
He was dirty, he had barely slept, his coat smelled of cellars.
She didn't seem to notice.
She poured him a cup he didn't touch.
"You found her," she said.
It wasn't a question.
He didn't answer.
"I'm going to tell you things as they are,"
Dross went on.
"You deserve that.
Seventeen months ago, a 7-B arrived on my desk.
Yours.
An agent's 7-B has to be countersigned by the Directorate, you know that.
I had already noticed that you'd been letting another file drag for three months.
A 7-B as well.
A woman.
It didn't take me long to understand."
She took a sip of tea.
"I executed hers.
I suspended yours.
And I sent you through Protocol D.
Four months was the minimum to make sure you wouldn't find the thread again.
Then you came back to the sixteenth, and you were better than ever.
I didn't do it against you, Kask.
I did it for you.
You don't throw away a man like you because he fell in love once."
"And the form?"
"I kept it.
You always keep documents.
You never know."
Kask looked at his own hands on the table.
They weren't shaking.
It surprised him.
"Why now?"
Dross set down her cup.
She picked up a tablet from her desk, switched it on, scrolled through something, and read in a neutral voice, without looking at the screen, as if reciting:
"November 2nd.
Existence check in Sector 9.
Subject consistent.
Report due at 9:07.
Report sent at 9:47."
She raised her eyes to him.
"Forty minutes.
You had never been a minute late in eleven years.
Not one.
That was the day I knew."
Kask didn't understand at first.
Then he saw the bench again, the delivery rider, the wind, the strand of hair tucked behind an ear with two fingers.
The missing step in the dark.
He hadn't thought about it since.
She had.
"Protocol D erases memories," said Dross.
"It doesn't erase the rest.
Sometimes the rest comes back.
I've seen it in others.
When it starts coming back, it doesn't stop.
There was the delay, and then you spent those ten days going home later than usual, always by the same street.
I waited a little.
Then I took the form out of the drawer."
"And I fell."
"You got what you asked for.
It was your signature, Kask.
Your decision.
Nobody investigates a 7-B.
All I did was execute it, a little late."
She smiled slightly, almost tenderly.
"And I had you flagged as reserved.
So they'd bring you back here, and not somewhere else."
Somewhere else.
Kask thought of the grey cars, of the man with the stove pushed in the back, of the glasses on the ground.
"What's behind the Gate?"
Dross looked at him for a moment, and he had the impression, for the first time, that she was genuinely thinking before she answered.
"I don't know," she said.
"It's not my department."
He believed her.
It was perhaps the most frightening thing she had ever said to him.
"Here's what I'm offering you," said Dross.
She folded her hands on the table.
"A second Protocol D.
Shorter, this time.
You'll forget these three days, and a few months either side, to be safe.
In exchange, I rectify your rectification.
It's rare, but I can do it.
Your name goes back into the Registry.
Your lodgings, your account, your badge.
Your book, if you care about it.
You go back to your post on the sixteenth on Monday, and Teodor will never have handled your file."
"And if not?"
"If not, you stay what you've been since last night at 23:40.
You go back down, if you like.
You live down there.
Collections aren't always as badly organized as last night's, and your face won't be reserved for anyone anymore."
"And her?"
"She doesn't interest me,"
Dross said simply.
Kask said nothing.
Outside, a Transport convoy was gliding slowly westward along the elevated track.
He watched it until it disappeared behind a tower.
"You're going to tell me you can't,"
Dross went on.
"That you know now, and you can't go back once you know.
They all say that.
But you won't know anymore, Kask.
That's the whole point.
In a week, you won't even remember hesitating."
She stood, and he understood the interview was over.
"You have until eight o'clock.
They're preparing a room for you.
Think it over, if that helps."
She put her hand on his shoulder as she passed, very briefly.
"They all come back up, you know."
The room was on the twentieth floor.
It was white and windowless.
A table, two chairs, a ceiling light that hummed on a very low note.
It was the same room as the one on the sixteenth, but for one detail: the door had no handle on this side.
Kask sat down on the chair where, for eleven years, he had made others sit.
He thought it over, as she had advised.
He thought of his lodgings, the pale grey walls, the terminal, the Atlas on the table.
He thought of Alley 11-C.
He thought that in a week, if he accepted, he might go that way again every evening, without knowing why, and stop in front of a wall, and turn back.
He thought of a tune whose ending he would never know again.
He also thought, and he was ashamed to think it, that it would be simpler.
That it would no longer hurt in that place.
That Dross was perhaps right, and that they all came back up.
Around seven, the light began to sputter.
Around half past seven, he heard footsteps in the corridor.
They stopped outside the door.
The door opened.
It wasn't the medical team.
It was Teodor, alone, a sheet of paper in his hand.
Teodor closed the door behind him and put the sheet on the table.
Kask recognized it before he even read it.
He had issued four hundred of them.
A departure permit, in the regulation format, with the Bureau seal in the top left corner.
Subject: KASK.
File R-88412. 10:00 convoy.
Gate Station.
At the bottom, the signature of the assigned agent.
Teodor's.
"I'm the agent on the file,"
Teodor said quietly.
"I'm the one who issues the permit.
That's the procedure."
"Dross has put a flag on me."
"In the Directorate's system.
The guards downstairs report to Security.
They check the permit, and the permit is valid."
He gave a small, tense smile.
"The departments don't talk to each other.
You used to say that was healthy."
Kask looked at the sheet, then at Teodor.
He searched for something to say to him.
He would have liked to explain what that signature at the bottom of a permit meant, what Dross would do when she saw it, in an hour or in a day.
He understood that Teodor didn't know.
He knew he was disobeying, that there would be a sanction, perhaps a transfer.
He knew nothing about Protocol D.
He didn't know the word.
He was doing it anyway.
"Come on," said Teodor.
They went down together.
The lift stopped at the fourteenth, then the ground floor.
In the lobby, two Security guards stood behind the gate, in navy-blue uniforms.
Teodor went through first, his badge lit.
Kask stepped up behind him and held out the permit.
The guard took it and passed it under a reader.
Kask watched the little screen on the other side of the counter and waited for it to turn orange.
It stayed green.
"Departure," said the guard, without looking up.
"Gate Station, ten o'clock convoy.
Keep this document on you until boarding."
He handed it back.
The gate opened.
Outside, the City was waking up.
People were passing on the pavement, hurried, eyes lowered, stepping slightly aside in front of the two dark coats.
The sky was white.
They walked a few steps to the corner of the tower, where they could no longer be seen from the lobby.
Teodor stopped.
So did Kask.
"Record yourself tonight," said Kask.
"Tell what you did today.
And why.
Then hide the recording."
Teodor frowned.
"Why?"
Kask thought of a bench in Sector 9, a strand of hair, a woman he hadn't recognized who had been waiting for him for sixteen months.
He thought of everything that ought to be said and that wouldn't fit into the minute they had left.
"Run your own existence check," he said.
Teodor looked at him for a long time.
He didn't understand, Kask could see that.
But something passed over his face, a shadow, an attentiveness.
He nodded.
"Bon voyage," he said.
He held out his hand.
Kask shook it.
Then Teodor turned and went back into the tower, and the gate closed behind him.
Kask never saw him again.
He didn't head for the station.
The permit let him through the checkpoints as far as the platforms, and he used it twice, at the Sector 9 and Sector 11 checkpoints, under the indifferent eyes of the officers.
Then he turned into Alley 11-C.
He passed the closed café.
The sign sputtered faintly in the daylight.
He walked to the end, to the wall, and for the first time in sixteen months he didn't turn back.
He pushed the wire-mesh door.
At the foot of the stairs, in front of terminal PB-14/3-07, he took the permit out of his pocket.
He folded it in two, laid it on top of the terminal, and left it there.
Nell was at Vay's.
She was sitting on a stool among the dead screens, a blanket around her shoulders.
When he parted the curtain of plastic strips, she stood up all at once.
She didn't come closer.
She looked him up and down, as if to check that he was whole, that he was himself, that he was there.
"They let you go?"
"No," said Kask.
Vay, bent over his workbench, took out his loupe.
"Sit down," he said.
"Before she asks you a second time."
He told them.
He did it without pride or apology, the way you take stock of an inventory.
With Kask's badge, during the hour he had bought, he had consulted the Sanitation schedules.
He did it every time he got his hands on an agent's badge.
It was the only way, down here, to know when and where the grey cars would come.
He had seen Founders' Passage on the list for the following night.
"You could have warned her," said Kask.
"I don't go down to Level −4 on the night of a collection.
You were going there anyway.
And you can read their cells.
I thought it was the best service I could do her."
He shrugged and looked at Nell.
"I owed her that.
Now we're even."
Nell said nothing.
But when she turned to Kask, it wasn't the same look as in the utility room at the end of the passage.
The suspicion was gone.
Everything else remained.
In the days that followed, Kask learned to live down below.
He learned simple things.
Which pipes you could open, and at what time.
How you paid for a meal with a repaired part.
How you kept quiet, and how you pressed yourself against a wall, when a drone passed too low.
Vay gave him small jobs in the workshop, terminals to strip, cables to sort.
He was better at taking things apart than at repairing them.
Vay said that was only natural, given his former line of work.
He had put his coat away.
He wore a jacket too big for him that someone had given him.
In the street, people still looked at him, but they didn't spit anymore.
One morning, the old man on the step gave him the same small nod as on the first evening.
This time there was no irony in it, or almost none.
They slept at Vay's, in the back room, on either side of a curtain.
Nell worked at the recycling workshop.
In the evenings they ate together, and spoke little.
She didn't tell him their story.
He didn't ask her to.
They both knew it wouldn't give him anything back.
One night, when he thought she was asleep, she spoke in the dark.
"I don't know if it's you."
He thought for a long time before answering.
"Neither do I."
She said nothing more.
He heard her turn over.
It wasn't what they had had, it was nothing he could name.
It was two people starting again from nothing, knowing they had loved each other once already, and that one of them had lost it.
But it was something.
On the ninth day, Vay called them into the workshop.
He looked embarrassed, which wasn't like him.
"I hesitated to tell you," he began.
"During the hour with the badge, I didn't only look at the Sanitation schedules.
I also opened the Transport registers.
The convoy manifests.
I was looking for other names, for other clients.
And then I remembered."
He turned a screen toward Nell.
One line was highlighted.
Kask recognized the format, and the file number.
It was his own.
The one he had processed more than three years ago: the man of twenty-six, the debt, the permit, the bon voyage.
Nell's brother.
The line didn't say he was dead.
It didn't say he had left.
It gave neither place nor date.
It ended with a single word, in the status column:
Assigned.
Nell looked at the screen without moving.
Kask was looking at the word.
He knew it.
He had heard it on the sixteenth for eleven years, from managers, in circulars, in speeches.
Nobody said an agent had been dismissed, or decompressed, or erased.
They said he had been reassigned.
Behind the Gate, perhaps they didn't kill people.
They used them.
Nell turned to him.
Her eyes were dry, very bright.
"Do you know what it means?"
Kask thought of Brenn behind his counter in Sector 6, who didn't remember the Bureau.
He thought of Halm, of his envelope, of his wet eyes.
He thought of Teodor, somewhere above their heads, who had perhaps, one evening, talked to himself in front of a recorder.
"Yes," he said.
